title: Helm Basics
intro: Helm is Kubernetes' package manager — instead of hand-writing and applying a dozen YAML files, you install a 'chart' that bundles them all with configurable values.

steps.prompt: Search the default Helm repo for a redis chart.
steps.fake_output:
NAME                CHART VERSION   APP VERSION
bitnami/redis       18.4.0          7.2.4
steps.explanation: This searches charts from repos you've already added locally with 'helm repo add' — it's not a live internet search.
steps.why: This is the Helm equivalent of browsing a package registry like npm or pip before installing — confirms the chart exists and which versions are available.

steps.prompt: Install that redis chart as a release named 'my-cache'.
steps.explanation: This one command creates every Kubernetes object the chart defines — Deployment, Service, Secret, etc — all at once, wired together per the chart's defaults.
steps.why: Doing this by hand would mean writing and applying several separate YAML manifests yourself, staying in sync with upstream's recommended config — the chart already encodes all of that.

steps.prompt: Override the default password by installing (or upgrading) with a custom value.
steps.fake_output: Release "my-cache" has been upgraded. Happy Helming!
steps.explanation: 'upgrade --install' is the idempotent form — it installs if the release doesn't exist yet, or upgrades it if it does, so the same command works either way.
steps.why: Plain 'helm install' would fail if 'my-cache' already exists — 'upgrade --install' is what you'd actually put in a CI/CD pipeline since it works whether this is the first deploy or the hundredth.

steps.prompt: Something's wrong after that change — roll the release back to revision 1.
steps.fake_output: Rollback was a success! Happy Helming!
steps.explanation: Like 'kubectl rollout undo' for Deployments, Helm keeps its own revision history per release so you can revert instantly.
steps.why: This reverts every object the chart manages back to that revision's state in one command — doing it manually would mean remembering and reapplying the old values for every object individually.
